strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: enabling cooperation (ensemble, distillation, speculative decoding) between LMs with mismatched vocabularies, with a principled alternative to heuristic cross-tokenizer ensembling.

The theoretical framework is clean and correct: the notion of nested tokenization yields a simple pushforward construction (Eq. 11), and Theorem 3.1 (losslessness) follows cleanly; generalizes the byte-level reduction of Phan et al. (2025)/Vieira et al. (2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies, with byte-level reduction as a special case.

Recursive computation (Theorem 3.4) with relative covering sets is a natural and non-trivial extension of the minimal-cover machinery, with proofs provided in the appendix and a fully worked illustrative example (Section 3.2/B) that aids understanding.
Efficient implementation (Algorithm 2) reduces the naive nested loops to a single pass plus a top-K loop, making the method practical with negligible overhead (K=300).

Experiments are reasonably thorough: five model families, four benchmarks, comparison against sensible baselines (naive restriction, union-vocabulary ensemble, byte-level ensemble), plus an inference-speed comparison showing MCV ensemble is ~2x faster than byte-level ensemble (Table 3).

Results support the claims: LVR preserves accuracy across sub-vocabulary sizes where naive restriction collapses, and LVR-based PoE ensembling avoids the catastrophic failures of heuristic baselines (Table 2/5/6). Honest treatment of greedy-decoding inconsistencies and a cherry-picked failure case (Table 7) is commendable.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core machinery (validity condition, minimal covering, next-byte computation) is inherited from Phan et al. (2025) and Vieira et al. (2025); the contribution is essentially generalizing bytes to an arbitrary sub-vocabulary, and Theorem 3.1 is a fairly straightforward consequence of composing pushforward distributions.

The 'lossless' claim is weakened in practice: the actually-used Algorithm 2 truncates to top-K tokens, so the deployed method is approximate. There is no theoretical or empirical analysis of the approximation error as a function of K, no ablation over K, and no discussion of when truncation may bias the distribution. Some results hint at non-trivial deviations (e.g., Falcon3-7B drops from 76.65 to 67.17 on 1-byte LVR; OLMo2-1B 'improves' from 30.40 to 31.46), which are not analyzed.

Efficiency costs of reduction itself are underexplored: generating with a reduced sub-vocabulary produces shorter tokens on average, requiring more iterations (and thus more forward passes and more relative-cover bookkeeping) than the original full-vocabulary model for the same text; the paper reports speedups only in the ensemble-vs-byte-ensemble comparison, not the overhead of LVR relative to the original model or vs. the byte-level reduction per step.

Ensemble experiments use only two models (N=2); scaling behavior of the maximal-common-vocabulary approach (which shrinks rapidly as more models are added) is untested, which is important since MCV size is the key quantity determining both accuracy and speed.

The maximal common vocabulary construction is somewhat ad hoc (BPE restricted to intersection), with acknowledged arbitrariness in the associated tokenizer; sensitivity to this choice is not examined.
No code release or artifact statement is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the algorithmic implementation despite the reproducibility statement.

Minor issues: typos ('valid tokens' grammar, 'performance'/'probabilityies', 'sicne'), and Table 7 shows substantive disagreement between reduced models of the same base model that deserves more discussion given the losslessness claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically relevant problem: enabling cooperation (ensemble, etc.) between language models with mismatched tokenizers at the next-token distribution level.

The formal framework is clean and clearly written; the definitions of nested tokenization and vocabulary reduction are well-motivated, and the byte-level reduction of Phan et al. (2025); Vieira et al. (2025) is correctly recovered as a special case.
The illustrative worked example (Sections 3.2 and B) is helpful and honestly points out subtleties, e.g., that greedy decoding is not preserved even under text-distribution equivalence.

The efficient algorithm (Algorithm 2) with top-K truncation is a sensible engineering contribution, and the ensemble experiments show clear speedups over byte-level ensemble (~1.8-2x bytes/sec) while matching or beating byte-level ensemble accuracy.

The paper is well positioned relative to prior work, with a related work section that clearly distinguishes theoretical (byte-level reduction) from heuristic (union vocabulary, embedding similarity) approaches.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is a fairly direct generalization of the minimal-cover/byte-level reduction machinery in Phan et al. (2025) and Vieira et al. (2025) from one-byte tokens to an arbitrary sub-vocabulary. The proofs (Lemmas A.1, A.2, Theorem 3.4) are mechanical extensions of existing results, and the claim of 'the first theoretical framework' is overstated given this lineage.

Internal tension between theory and the actual algorithm: the theoretical results are exact ('lossless'), but the practical Algorithm 2 uses top-K truncation of the vocabulary, which breaks the losslessness guarantee. The paper provides no analysis or measurement of the approximation error introduced by K=300, no ablation over K, and no justification that the error is 'negligible' beyond a single sentence. This weakens the central claim.

The per-step computational overhead of LVR (re-tokenization, relative-cover bookkeeping, cache maintenance) is never quantified or compared against the overhead of the byte-level baseline; the reported bytes/sec comparison conflates token length with algorithmic overhead.

Evaluation is narrow: vocabulary-reduction experiments use only GSM8K; ensemble experiments use only two models (Qwen2.5-3B + Falcon3-7B, plus a smaller pair in the appendix); several benchmarks are subsampled to only 100 questions per category, making small differences (e.g., Falcon3-7B LVR 78.92 vs. Full 76.65) hard to interpret and suggesting noise. Anomalies where LVR improves over the full model are unexplained.

Greedy decoding is not invariant under vocabulary reduction (acknowledged in Section B), so 'no loss in accuracy' holds only for the text distribution, not for the decoded outputs; the paper's framing at times glosses over this distinction, and Table 7 shows reduced models disagreeing on final answers.

The construction of the maximal common vocabulary and its associated BPE tokenizer (Equation 25) inherits tokenization bias from the first tokenizer, and the impact of this arbitrary choice is not studied.
No code release is mentioned, and reproducibility details for the cache/cover-computation implementation are thin.

Significance is somewhat limited: the benefit over existing byte-level reduction (Phan et al., 2025) is a constant-factor speedup for cross-vocabulary ensembling, a relatively narrow use case; other downstream applications enabled by arbitrary sub-vocabulary reduction are not demonstrated.

strengths: The paper establishes a clean, well-formalized theoretical framework for lossless vocabulary reduction that meaningfully generalizes prior byte-level reduction work (Phan et al. 2025; Vieira et al. 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies; the nested tokenization construction and the recursive computation via relative coverings (Theorem 3.4) are technically sound, with proofs provided in the appendix.

The application to ensembling over the maximal common vocabulary is a natural and practical contribution: it provides a principled alternative to heuristic cross-vocabulary ensemble methods (union vocabulary, embedding-similarity matching) that lack theoretical guarantees, and the empirical results show the heuristics can catastrophically fail (e.g., MMLU-Pro with PoE) while LVR remains robust.

Experiments cover multiple model families (OLMo2, Llama3.2, Qwen2.5, Falcon3) and multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, MMLU-Pro), with both PoE and MoE ensembling; the inference-speed comparison (Table 3) confirms the expected efficiency advantage over byte-level ensemble (~2x bytes/sec).

The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly acknowledges and analyzes the greedy-decoding inconsistency between distributionally-equivalent models (Section B) and even includes a cherry-picked negative example (Table 7) where reduced models disagree.
The illustrative worked example (Sections 3.2/B) makes the somewhat abstract theory concrete and verifiable, and both a naive and an efficient algorithm are provided, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core machinery (validity condition, minimal covering, marginalization to sub-alphabets) is largely inherited from Phan et al. (2025) and Vieira et al. (2025); the contribution is primarily a generalization from bytes to arbitrary sub-vocabularies, which is elegant but a fairly natural extension, and the proofs are short adaptations of prior lemmas.

The 'lossless' claim is undermined by the practical algorithm: Algorithm 2 truncates to top-K=300 tokens for tractability, which makes the method approximate in exactly the way the byte-level reduction in Phan et al. is not; no theoretical or empirical analysis of the approximation error (e.g., how accuracy degrades with K) is provided, and the paper does not clearly separate exact vs. approximate guarantees in its claims.

Evaluation is somewhat narrow: the vocabulary-reduction experiments are only on GSM8K with greedy decoding; only 2-model ensembles are tested; the MCV ensemble requires substantial tokenizer overlap (63K/151K shared tokens between Qwen and Falcon), and the behavior for models with small or disjoint common vocabularies is not explored.

Some reported numbers are anomalous and under-explained, e.g., LVR exceeding the full-vocabulary model (78.92 vs. 76.65 for Falcon3-7B), which likely reflects greedy path deviation but is not analyzed; also LVR (1-Byte) frequently outperforms LVR (MCV), raising questions about when the extra complexity of MCV is worthwhile beyond throughput.

The practical overhead of LVR (re-tokenization, maintaining cover caches, per-step Python-level bookkeeping vs. the single softmax of the baseline) is not reported for single-model reduction experiments; efficiency is only quantified for the ensemble setting.

The effective speedup over byte-level ensemble depends on the average byte-length of tokens in the common vocabulary, which is dataset/domain dependent; the significance of the practical gain may be narrower than the framing suggests.

strengths: The paper establishes a clean and correct generalization of recent byte-level reduction methods (Phan et al., 2025; Vieira et al., 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies via the notion of nested tokenization and relative coverings; the theory (Theorem 3.1, Lemmas 3.2-3.4) is sound, and proofs are provided in the appendix.

The derived algorithm is practical: the top-K approximation (K-LVR) keeps overhead small (analyzed in Section D.7.3), and ablations over K (Tables 12-14) show the method is robust for greedy decoding and needs larger K under sampling, which is a thoughtful and honest analysis.

The application to ensembling over the maximal common vocabulary (MCV) is well motivated and empirically supported: it matches or beats byte-level ensemble accuracy (Tables 2, 5, 6, 8) while being substantially faster (Table 3), and it avoids the catastrophic failures of heuristic baselines (Union, Naive) under product-of-experts ensembling.

Evaluation covers multiple models (Qwen, OLMo, Llama, Falcon, Phi, Yi) and multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, MMLU-Pro, WMT translation), including both greedy and temperature-1.0 sampling settings.

The paper is transparent about subtleties, e.g., that greedy decoding of a distribution-equivalent model can produce different texts (Section B), and includes a cherry-picked failure example (Table 7).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the framework is a fairly direct extension of the minimal-covering machinery of Phan et al. (2025) and Vieira et al. (2025) from bytes to sub-vocabularies; the core idea (marginalizing next-token probabilities over re-tokenizations) is already present in prior work, and the losslessness theorem follows almost immediately from the prior Lemma 2.1 applied to nested tokenization.

The efficient Algorithm 2 is an approximation, so the practical method does not actually enjoy the 'lossless' guarantee; notably, K=1 suffices for greedy decoding (Table 12), suggesting the empirical gains may come more from the approximation behaving like naive retokenization than from the full theory.

The evaluation of vocabulary reduction in the main text is limited to GSM8K; other benchmarks appear only for ensembling, and there is no perplexity-based or distributional divergence measure to directly quantify how well the reduced model matches the original (beyond end-task accuracy).

The ensemble experiments only use pairs of two models; no experiments with more than two models, and the MCV construction is acknowledged to be arbitrary (based on the first tokenizer's BPE pairs), with no ablation of this choice.

The claimed advantage over byte-level ensembling (fewer generation steps) is somewhat expected by construction, since MCV tokens are longer than bytes; a more rigorous end-to-end wall-clock and memory comparison would strengthen the efficiency claim.

Some potential applications mentioned in the introduction (distillation, speculative decoding, inference-time alignment) are not explored, so the demonstrated scope is narrower than the framing suggests.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: enabling language models with different tokenizers/vocabularies to cooperate (e.g., ensembling) at the next-token distribution level.

The theoretical framework is clearly formulated. The nested tokenization construction is clean, the losslessness theorem (Theorem 3.1) is correct, and the reduction of Phan et al. (2025)'s byte-level method to a special case (Vsub = A) is properly identified.
The derivation from exact but infeasible Algorithm 1 to the practical top-K approximation (Algorithm 2) is well motivated, with concrete complexity analysis of the two nested loops.

The experimental section is relatively thorough for the core claim: vocabulary reduction is validated across multiple model families (OLMo2, Llama3.2, Qwen2.5, Falcon3) with a sensible naive-restriction baseline, ablations on K (Tables 12-14), temperature-1.0 evaluation (Table 11), PoE vs. MoE ensembles (Tables 5-6), additional model pairs (Table 8), and translation tasks (Table 9).
The demonstration that MCV-based ensemble is ~1.5-2x faster than byte-level ensemble (Table 3) while achieving comparable accuracy is a concrete practical benefit over the prior byte-level approach.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over the closely related concurrent work. The core contribution is essentially a generalization of Phan et al. (2025) and Vieira et al. (2025) from bytes to arbitrary sub-vocabularies under the validity assumption, which the paper itself concedes (Section 6). Given that byte-level LVR already exists and the mathematical machinery (relative covers, validity condition) is directly inherited, the incremental step may not clear the bar for a top-tier venue.

Tension between the 'lossless' claim and the empirical results. If the reduction were truly behavior-preserving, greedy decoding should produce (near-)identical outputs and accuracy should match the original model. Instead, K-LVR consistently improves over the original model by ~2-3 points across all token lengths (e.g., Falcon3-7B: 76.65 -> 79.3 under greedy; 47.54 -> 47.61 under sampling), and the ensemble results also exceed the single models. This systematic discrepancy is not convincingly explained and suggests the practical pipeline is not actually behavior-preserving, undermining the central 'without any loss in accuracy' narrative.

The exact (lossless) algorithm is computationally infeasible, and the practical K-LVR approximation comes with no error analysis or theoretical bound (e.g., KL divergence between the approximated and exact reduced distributions). The claim of 'negligibly small overhead' / near-losslessness is supported only empirically, and the fixed K=300 choice is not justified; Table 13 shows that under sampling even K=1250 deviates noticeably from the original distribution (47.61 vs. 47.54, with large swings at intermediate K).

The construction of the tokenizer for the maximal common vocabulary is ad hoc: it inherits BPE merges from the first tokenizer T1 only. The paper provides no analysis of how sensitive the reduced models' quality is to this choice, even though losslessness is only guaranteed relative to this arbitrary nested tokenization.

Missing comparisons with other lines of cross-vocabulary ensembling baselines. The empirical comparison is restricted to Union (Yao et al., 2025) and Naive(MCV); the partial-matching (Jiang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025) and embedding-similarity (Xu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024) approaches discussed in Related Work are dismissed qualitatively ('no theoretical guarantee') but never compared against empirically, leaving the practical superiority claim incomplete.

The main-text experiments are narrow (primarily GSM8K for vocabulary reduction; a single model pair for the headline ensemble table), with the broader evidence relegated to the appendix. Some results (e.g., MATH accuracy of K-LVR ensembles dropping below single-model performance, Table 5/6) are not analyzed.

Greedy-decoding discrepancies are acknowledged (Section B) but downplayed; given that most reported main results use greedy decoding, and greedy decoding is not distribution-preserving under the reduction, the headline accuracy numbers measure something other than the theoretical property the paper emphasizes.

No code release or reproducibility artifact is mentioned beyond the reproducibility statement pointing to experimental details, which limits verifiability of the nontrivial implementation (caching, relative covers, top-K approximation).

strengths: The paper generalizes the recent byte-level reduction framework (Phan et al., 2025; Vieira et al., 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies, which is a natural and useful extension: it enables model cooperation (e.g., ensemble) over the maximal common vocabulary rather than bytes, retaining theoretical guarantees while improving inference efficiency (Table 3 shows ~2x higher bytes/sec vs. byte-level ensemble).

The theoretical development is clean and self-contained: the nested tokenization and relative covering notions cleanly recover the byte-level case as a special case (V_sub = A), the lossless property (Theorem 3.1) is straightforwardly proven, and the recursive decomposition (Lemmas 3.2-3.4, Appendix A) is correct to the best of my assessment.
The paper is honest about the subtlety that lossless text distributions do not imply identical greedy decodings (Section B / footnote 7), which many authors would have glossed over.

Empirically comprehensive for the claims made: multiple model families (Qwen, Llama, OLMo, Falcon, Phi, Yi), multiple benchmarks, both PoE and MoE ensembles, translation evaluation, sampling-temperature evaluation, and a thorough ablation on K (Tables 12-14, Figure 4).
The top-K approximation is well-motivated and analyzed; the ablations show K=1 suffices for greedy decoding while larger K is needed for faithful sampling, which is an informative distinction.

Experiments support the central claims: K-LVR preserves accuracy under vocabulary reduction (Table 1) and outperforms heuristic baselines (Union, Naive MCV) on ensemble, matching byte-level ensemble accuracy while being faster.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core machinery (validity condition, minimal covering, marginalization over valid tokenizations) is directly inherited from Phan et al. (2025) and Vieira et al. (2025); the contribution is essentially a generalization from bytes to arbitrary sub-vocabularies, and the theory amounts to re-deriving the covering argument for this setting. Given three closely related concurrent works (Phan et al., Vieira et al., Hayase et al.), the incremental step should be stated more carefully.

A gap exists between the headline 'lossless' claim and the practical method: K-LVR is an approximation, and Table 1 shows reduced models scoring above the original (e.g., Falcon3-7B 78.92 vs 76.65 full), indicating approximation/decoding-path effects rather than strict equivalence. The paper should more clearly separate exact LVR (computationally infeasible) from the deployed approximation.

The catastrophic failure of the Union baseline (e.g., 1.93 on MMLU-Pro in Table 2, 2.58 in Table 5) is suspicious relative to prior reports that union-vocabulary ensemble works reasonably well (Yao et al., 2025); this makes the relative gains over baselines harder to interpret and needs verification/justification.

Evaluation scale is modest: MATH, ACPBench, and MMLU-Pro use only 100 sampled questions per category; the main paper results focus on GSM8K. The sampled subsets introduce nontrivial variance that is not quantified (no error bars/seeds).

Overhead analysis for the single-model vocabulary reduction is incomplete: the paper reports ensemble bytes/sec (Table 3), but not the wall-clock or memory overhead of K-LVR relative to plain generation (per-step top-K loop, cache management, retokenization), which matters for the practicality claim.

No code release is mentioned; the reproducibility statement is thin, which is a concern given the method depends on many implementation details (caching, tokenizer implementations, greedy decoding tie-breaking).

The application scope is mostly demonstrated on PoE/MoE ensembling; other motivating use cases (knowledge distillation, speculative decoding, inference-time alignment) listed in the introduction are not explored.

Some writing issues: the claim 'first theoretical framework of lossless vocabulary reduction' is repeated but is partly a definitional matter given prior byte-level work; minor grammatical errors ('is a valid tokens', 'probabilityies', 'perfomance', 'ocurred').
